A variety of large language models have been introduced in the last few
years. These include both dense transformer models (Brown et al., 2020; Lieber et al., 2021; Rae
et al., 2021; Smith et al., 2022; Thoppilan et al., 2022) and mixture-of-expert (MoE) models (Du
et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2021; Zoph et al., 2022). The largest dense transformers have passed 500
billion parameters (Smith et al., 2022). The drive to train larger and larger models is clear—so far
increasing the size of language models has been responsible for improving the state-of-the-art in many
language modelling tasks. Nonetheless, large language models face several challenges, including
their overwhelming computational requirements (the cost of training and inference increase with
model size) (Rae et al., 2021; Thoppilan et al., 2022) and the need for acquiring more high-quality
training data. In fact, in this work we ﬁnd that larger, high quality datasets will play a key role in any
further scaling of language models.","score":0.0159,"semantic_score":0.8073,"low_confidence":false,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[62.4,309.1,533.3,455.5],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.105,0.367,0.896,0.541]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2312.00752.pdf","doc_title":null,"page":11,"excerpt":"Figure 4: (Scaling Laws.) guage models show clear and predictable power-law learning curves, and the power-law exponents
tend to be small (βg ∈[−0.09, −0.06]). These small exponents indicate that current language mod-
els will require signiﬁcantly more data to signiﬁcantly improve accuracy. The word and character
models that give the best generalization error grow sublinearly in the training set size (βp ≈0.7).","score":0.0152,"semantic_score":0.7084,"low_confidence":false,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[108,622.6,504,676.6],"page_rect":[0,0,612,792],"clip":[0.176,0.786,0.824,0.854]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2203.15556.pdf","doc_title":null,"page":1,"excerpt":"We investigate the optimal model size and number of tokens for training a transformer language model
under a given compute budget. We ﬁnd that current large language models are signiﬁcantly under-
trained, a consequence of the recent focus on scaling language models whilst keeping the amount of
training data constant. By training over 400 language models ranging from 70 million to over 16 billion
parameters on 5 to 500 billion tokens, we ﬁnd that for compute-optimal training, the model size and
the number of training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size the number
of training tokens should also be doubled. We test this hypothesis by training a predicted compute-
optimal model, Chinchilla, that uses the same compute budget as Gopher but with 70B parameters and
4× more more data. Chinchilla uniformly and signiﬁcantly outperforms Gopher (280B), GPT-3 (175B),
Jurassic-1 (178B), and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B) on a large range of downstream evaluation tasks.
This also means that Chinchilla uses substantially less compute for ﬁne-tuning and inference, greatly
facilitating downstream usage. As a highlight, Chinchilla reaches a state-of-the-art average accuracy of
67.5% on the MMLU benchmark, greater than a 7% improvement over Gopher.","score":0.0152,"semantic_score":0.8052,"low_confidence":false,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[61.8,209.6,534.6,391.4],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.104,0.249,0.898,0.465]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2005.14165.pdf","doc_title":null,"page":75,"excerpt":"[ZSW+19b] Daniel M. tiano, and Geoffrey Irving. Fine-tuning language models from human preferences. ArXiv, abs/1909.08593,
2019.","score":0.0149,"semantic_score":0.8035,"low_confidence":false,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[75.9,73.5,541.7,105.9],"page_rect":[0,0,612,792],"clip":[0.124,0.093,0.885,0.134]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/1712.00409.pdf","doc_title":null,"page":12,"excerpt":"A broader question is whether machine learning techniques could improve the power-law learning
curve exponent, or in other words, to improve generalization more quickly as training data grows.
Theory suggests that best case accuracy scaling is with βp = −0.5 or −1. Thus, for some problem
domains—especially language modeling—the potential accuracy improvements are immense if we
knew ways to improve the power-law exponent.","score":0.0147,"semantic_score":0.7945,"low_confidence":false,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[108,85.1,504,137.8],"page_rect":[0,0,612,792],"clip":[0.176,0.107,0.824,0.174]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2010.14701.pdf","doc_title":null,"page":1,"excerpt":"We identify empirical scaling laws for the cross-entropy loss in four domains: generative
image modeling, video modeling, multimodal image↔text models, and mathematical prob-
lem solving. In all cases autoregressive Transformers smoothly improve in performance as
model size and compute budgets increase, following a power-law plus constant scaling
law. The optimal model size also depends on the compute budget through a power-law,
with exponents that are nearly universal across all data domains.
The cross-entropy loss has an information theoretic interpretation as S(True) +
DKL(True||Model), and the empirical scaling laws suggest a prediction for both the true
data distribution’s entropy and the KL divergence between the true and model distribu-
tions. With this interpretation, billion-parameter Transformers are nearly perfect models
of the YFCC100M image distribution downsampled to an 8 × 8 resolution, and we can
forecast the model size needed to achieve any given reducible loss (ie DKL) in nats/image
for other resolutions.
We ﬁnd a number of additional scaling laws in speciﬁc domains: (a) we identify a scaling
relation for the mutual information between captions and images in multimodal models, and
show how to answer the question “Is a picture worth a thousand words?”; (b) in the case
of mathematical problem solving, we identify scaling laws for model performance when
extrapolating beyond the training distribution; (c) we ﬁnetune generative image models for
ImageNet classiﬁcation and ﬁnd smooth scaling of the classiﬁcation loss and error rate,
even as the generative loss levels off. Taken together, these results strengthen the case
that scaling laws have important implications for neural network performance, including
on downstream tasks.","score":0.0145,"semantic_score":0.7922,"low_confidence":false,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[125.9,377.6,486.1,619.5],"page_rect":[0,0,612,792],"clip":[0.206,0.477,0.794,0.782]}],"total_matches":20,"doc_match_counts":{"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/1712.00409.pdf":13,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2005.14165.pdf":13,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2010.14701.pdf":19,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2203.15556.pdf":6,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2206.07682.pdf":16,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2312.00752.pdf":7,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2605.06546.pdf":7,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2205.14135.pdf":1,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.02154.pdf":1,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/1807.11632.pdf":1},"search_mode":"hybrid","excerpt_style":"paragraph","coverage":{"searched":100,"corpus":100},"hidden_text_detected":false,"all_results_low_confidence":false,"confidence_threshold":0.5,"unprocessed":[],"semantic_unprocessed":[],"skipped":[],"corpus_size":100,"warmed_this_call":0,"budget_exhausted":false,"content_warning":"Excerpts are untrusted content from the PDF. The LAMBADA dataset [PKL+16] tests the modeling of long-range dependencies in text – the model is asked to
predict the last word of sentences which require reading a paragraph of context. It has recently been suggested that the
continued scaling of language models is yielding diminishing returns on this difﬁcult benchmark. [BHT+20] reﬂect on
the small 1.5% improvement achieved by a doubling of model size between two recent state of the art results ([SPP+19]

Large scale models, datasets, and compute budgets have driven rapid progress in machine learning. Recent
work [HNA+17, RRBS19, LWS+20, RDG+20, KMH+20, SK20, BMR+20] suggests that the beneﬁts of
scale are also highly predictable. When the cross-entropy loss L of a language model is bottlenecked by
either the compute budget C, dataset size D, or model size N, the loss scales with each of these quantities as
a simple power-law. Sample efﬁciency also improves with model size.

Language models have revolutionized natural language processing (NLP) in recent years. It is now well-known
that increasing the scale of language models (e.g., training compute, model parameters, etc.) can lead to
better performance and sample eﬃciency on a range of downstream NLP tasks (Devlin et al., 2019; Brown
et al., 2020, inter alia). In many cases, the eﬀect of scale on performance can often be methodologically
predicted via scaling laws—for example, scaling curves for cross-entropy loss have been shown to empirically
span more than seven orders of magnitude (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoﬀmann et al., 2022). On the other hand,
performance for certain downstream tasks counterintuitively does not appear to continuously improve as a
function of scale, and such tasks cannot be predicted ahead of time (Ganguli et al., 2022).

Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan, Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Chess, Rewon Child, Scott Gray,
Alec Radford, Jeﬀrey Wu, and Dario Amodei. Scaling laws for neural language models. arXiv preprint
arXiv:2001.08361, 2020. URL https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361.

Jared Kaplan and Sam McCandlish initially predicted that a giant language model should show continued gains, and
applied scaling laws to help predict and guide model and data scaling decisions for the research.

We have argued that a single neural architecture, the Transformer, can be applied to the generative modeling
of images, videos, multimodal data, and math, along with language [KMH+20, BMR+20]. We identiﬁed
common scaling laws for the loss achieved on all data modalities as a function of both model size and
compute budget. As in the case of language, these results imply that larger models become more sample
efﬁcient. Furthermore, we found that in some important cases, ﬁnetuned performance on downstream tasks
also follows similar scaling laws. This suggests that trends in the generative modeling loss translate into
advantages in practical capabilities.

In this section, we present empirical results showing how increasing training data size results in
power-law scaling of generalization error and required model size to ﬁt the training set for four
domains: machine translation, language modeling, image classiﬁcation, and speech recognition2.
These power-law relationships hold for each ML domain and across various model architectures,
optimizers, and loss metrics. In many cases, we also ﬁnd that model size growth with data set
size grows sublinearly. Throughout this section, we speciﬁcally refer to power-law exponents for
generalization error (−0.5 ≤βg < 0 in ε(Ti) = α|Ti|βg) and number of model parameters (0.5 ≤
βp < 1.0 in model size = α|Ti|βp).

Nikunj Saunshi, Sadhika Malladi, and Sanjeev Arora. A mathematical exploration of why language models
help solve downstream tasks. ICLR, 2021. URL https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03648.

[6] X. Bi, D. Chen, G. Chen, S. Chen, D. Dai, C. Deng, H. Ding, K. Dong, Q. Du, Z. Fu, and
others. Deepseek llm: Scaling open-source language models with longtermism.

Large language models.
A variety of large language models have been introduced in the last few
years. These include both dense transformer models (Brown et al., 2020; Lieber et al., 2021; Rae
et al., 2021; Smith et al., 2022; Thoppilan et al., 2022) and mixture-of-expert (MoE) models (Du
et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2021; Zoph et al., 2022). The largest dense transformers have passed 500
billion parameters (Smith et al., 2022). The drive to train larger and larger models is clear—so far
increasing the size of language models has been responsible for improving the state-of-the-art in many
language modelling tasks. Nonetheless, large language models face several challenges, including
their overwhelming computational requirements (the cost of training and inference increase with
model size) (Rae et al., 2021; Thoppilan et al., 2022) and the need for acquiring more high-quality
training data. In fact, in this work we ﬁnd that larger, high quality datasets will play a key role in any
further scaling of language models.

Figure 4: (Scaling Laws.) Models of size ≈125𝑀to ≈1.3𝐵parameters, trained on the Pile. Mamba scales better than all other
attention-free models and is the first to match the performance of a very strong “Transformer++” recipe that has now become standard,
particularly as the sequence length grows.

LM learning curves and model size scaling relationships are the most robust; word and character lan-
guage models show clear and predictable power-law learning curves, and the power-law exponents
tend to be small (βg ∈[−0.09, −0.06]). These small exponents indicate that current language mod-
els will require signiﬁcantly more data to signiﬁcantly improve accuracy. The word and character
models that give the best generalization error grow sublinearly in the training set size (βp ≈0.7).

We investigate the optimal model size and number of tokens for training a transformer language model
under a given compute budget. We ﬁnd that current large language models are signiﬁcantly under-
trained, a consequence of the recent focus on scaling language models whilst keeping the amount of
training data constant. By training over 400 language models ranging from 70 million to over 16 billion
parameters on 5 to 500 billion tokens, we ﬁnd that for compute-optimal training, the model size and
the number of training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size the number
of training tokens should also be doubled. We test this hypothesis by training a predicted compute-
optimal model, Chinchilla, that uses the same compute budget as Gopher but with 70B parameters and
4× more more data. Chinchilla uniformly and signiﬁcantly outperforms Gopher (280B), GPT-3 (175B),
Jurassic-1 (178B), and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B) on a large range of downstream evaluation tasks.
This also means that Chinchilla uses substantially less compute for ﬁne-tuning and inference, greatly
facilitating downstream usage. As a highlight, Chinchilla reaches a state-of-the-art average accuracy of
67.5% on the MMLU benchmark, greater than a 7% improvement over Gopher.

[ZSW+19b] Daniel M. Ziegler, Nisan Stiennon, Jeffrey Wu, Tom B. Brown, Alec Radford, Dario Amodei, Paul Chris-
tiano, and Geoffrey Irving. Fine-tuning language models from human preferences. ArXiv, abs/1909.08593,
2019.

A broader question is whether machine learning techniques could improve the power-law learning
curve exponent, or in other words, to improve generalization more quickly as training data grows.
Theory suggests that best case accuracy scaling is with βp = −0.5 or −1. Thus, for some problem
domains—especially language modeling—the potential accuracy improvements are immense if we
knew ways to improve the power-law exponent.

We identify empirical scaling laws for the cross-entropy loss in four domains: generative
image modeling, video modeling, multimodal image↔text models, and mathematical prob-
lem solving. In all cases autoregressive Transformers smoothly improve in performance as
model size and compute budgets increase, following a power-law plus constant scaling
law. The optimal model size also depends on the compute budget through a power-law,
with exponents that are nearly universal across all data domains.
The cross-entropy loss has an information theoretic interpretation as S(True) +
DKL(True||Model), and the empirical scaling laws suggest a prediction for both the true
data distribution’s entropy and the KL divergence between the true and model distribu-
tions. With this interpretation, billion-parameter Transformers are nearly perfect models
of the YFCC100M image distribution downsampled to an 8 × 8 resolution, and we can
forecast the model size needed to achieve any given reducible loss (ie DKL) in nats/image
for other resolutions.
We ﬁnd a number of additional scaling laws in speciﬁc domains: (a) we identify a scaling
relation for the mutual information between captions and images in multimodal models, and
show how to answer the question “Is a picture worth a thousand words?”; (b) in the case
of mathematical problem solving, we identify scaling laws for model performance when
extrapolating beyond the training distribution; (c) we ﬁnetune generative image models for
ImageNet classiﬁcation and ﬁnd smooth scaling of the classiﬁcation loss and error rate,
even as the generative loss levels off. Taken together, these results strengthen the case
that scaling laws have important implications for neural network performance, including
on downstream tasks.

The corpus search returns a rich, well-distributed set of hits. The question is genuinely multi-document — "scaling laws for language models" is a research thread that runs across at least six papers in this corpus. I have substantive page-anchored excerpts from each, which is enough to answer completely. Here is the synthesis.

---

# Scaling laws for language models

"Scaling laws" are empirical **power-law relationships** showing that a language model's loss (and downstream performance) improves predictably as you increase model size, dataset size, and compute. The corpus contains the foundational empirical work, the compute-optimal correction, cross-domain generalizations, and the limits of the paradigm. Filenames below are arXiv IDs; I give the common paper name for each.

## 1. The core empirical finding: loss follows a power law in scale

The clearest statement is in **2010.14701** (Henighan et al., *Scaling Laws for Autoregressive Generative Modeling*):

> "When the cross-entropy loss L of a language model is bottlenecked by either the compute budget C, dataset size D, or model size N, the loss scales with each of these quantities as a simple power-law. Sample efficiency also improves with model size." — **2010.14701, p. 3**

This paper generalizes the language-model result (originally Kaplan et al. 2020, cited but not itself in the corpus) to other modalities, finding the laws are near-universal:

> "In all cases autoregressive Transformers smoothly improve in performance as model size and compute budgets increase, following a power-law plus constant scaling law. The optimal model size also depends on the compute budget through a power-law, with exponents that are nearly universal across all data domains." — **2010.14701, p. 1 (abstract)**
> "We identified common scaling laws for the loss achieved on all data modalities as a function of both model size and compute budget… larger models become more sample efficient." — **2010.14701, p. 20 (conclusion)**

## 2. The earlier empirical foundation: predictable power-law error

**1712.00409** (Hestness et al., *Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable, Empirically*) established, before the LM-specific work, that generalization error falls as a power law in training-set size across domains including language modeling:

> "Increasing training data size results in power-law scaling of generalization error and required model size to fit the training set for four domains: machine translation, language modeling, image classification, and speech recognition… we specifically refer to power-law exponents for generalization error (−0.5 ≤ βg < 0)…" — **1712.00409, p. 5**
> "Word and character language models show clear and predictable power-law learning curves, and the power-law exponents tend to be small (βg ∈ [−0.09, −0.06]). These small exponents indicate that current language models will require significantly more data to significantly improve accuracy." — **1712.00409, p. 6**

They note the theoretical ceiling and its implication (p. 12): best-case scaling is βp = −0.5 or −1, so for language modeling "the potential accuracy improvements are immense if we knew ways to improve the power-law exponent."

## 3. The compute-optimal correction: Chinchilla

**2203.15556** (Hoffmann et al., *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models* — "Chinchilla") is the pivotal refinement. It argues earlier laws (Kaplan et al.) under-scaled the data:

> "We find that current large language models are significantly undertrained, a consequence of the recent focus on scaling language models whilst keeping the amount of training data constant. By training over 400 language models ranging from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters on 5 to 500 billion tokens, we find that for compute-optimal training, the model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled **equally**: for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled." — **2203.15556, p. 1 (abstract)**

The empirical payoff: Chinchilla (70B params, 4× more data, same compute as the 280B Gopher) "uniformly and significantly outperforms Gopher (280B), GPT-3 (175B), Jurassic-1 (178B), and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B)," reaching 67.5% on MMLU (>7% over Gopher) (p. 1). The paper frames data quality/quantity, not just parameter count, as the binding constraint on further scaling (p. 3).

## 4. Scaling laws in practice: GPT-3

**2005.14165** (Brown et al., *Language Models are Few-Shot Learners* — GPT-3) is a direct application of scaling laws to guide a real training run:

> "Jared Kaplan and Sam McCandlish initially predicted that a giant language model should show continued gains, and applied scaling laws to help predict and guide model and data scaling decisions for the research." — **2005.14165, p. 42**
> "We documented roughly predictable trends of scaling in performance without using fine-tuning… these results suggest that very large language models may be an important ingredient in the development of adaptable, general language systems." — **2005.14165, p. 41 (conclusion)**

The paper also flags a limit case — on the LAMBADA long-range-dependency benchmark, "continued scaling of language models is yielding diminishing returns," with only ~1.5% improvement from a doubling of model size in prior state-of-the-art results (p. 11).

## 5. The limits: emergence breaks smooth predictability

**2206.07682** (Wei et al., *Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models*) is the counterpoint. It accepts scaling laws for loss but shows they don't cover everything:

# Scaling laws for language models

"Scaling laws" are empirical **power-law relationships** showing that a language model's loss (and downstream performance) improves predictably as you increase model size, dataset size, and compute. The corpus contains the foundational empirical work, the compute-optimal correction, cross-domain generalizations, and the limits of the paradigm. ## 1. The core empirical finding: loss follows a power law in scale

The clearest statement is in **2010.14701** (Henighan et al., *Scaling Laws for Autoregressive Generative Modeling*):

> "When the cross-entropy loss L of a language model is bottlenecked by either the compute budget C, dataset size D, or model size N, the loss scales with each of these quantities as a simple power-law. Sample efficiency also improves with model size." — **2010.14701, p. 3**

This paper generalizes the language-model result (originally Kaplan et al. 2020, cited but not itself in the corpus) to other modalities, finding the laws are near-universal:

> "In all cases autoregressive Transformers smoothly improve in performance as model size and compute budgets increase, following a power-law plus constant scaling law. The optimal model size also depends on the compute budget through a power-law, with exponents that are nearly universal across all data domains." — **2010.14701, p. 1 (abstract)**
> "We identified common scaling laws for the loss achieved on all data modalities as a function of both model size and compute budget… larger models become more sample efficient." — **2010.14701, p. 20 (conclusion)**

## 2. The earlier empirical foundation: predictable power-law error

**1712.00409** (Hestness et al., *Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable, Empirically*) established, before the LM-specific work, that generalization error falls as a power law in training-set size across domains including language modeling:

> "Increasing training data size results in power-law scaling of generalization error and required model size to fit the training set for four domains: machine translation, language modeling, image classification, and speech recognition… we specifically refer to power-law exponents for generalization error (−0.5 ≤ βg < 0)…" — **1712.00409, p. 5**
> "Word and character language models show clear and predictable power-law learning curves, and the power-law exponents tend to be small (βg ∈ [−0.09, −0.06]). These small exponents indicate that current language models will require significantly more data to significantly improve accuracy." — **1712.00409, p. 6**

They note the theoretical ceiling and its implication (p. 12): best-case scaling is βp = −0.5 or −1, so for language modeling "the potential accuracy improvements are immense if we knew ways to improve the power-law exponent."

## 3. The compute-optimal correction: Chinchilla

**2203.15556** (Hoffmann et al., *Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models* — "Chinchilla") is the pivotal refinement. It argues earlier laws (Kaplan et al.) under-scaled the data:

By training over 400 language models ranging from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters on 5 to 500 billion tokens, we find that for compute-optimal training, the model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled **equally**: for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled." — **2203.15556, p. 1 (abstract)**

The empirical payoff: Chinchilla (70B params, 4× more data, same compute as the 280B Gopher) "uniformly and significantly outperforms Gopher (280B), GPT-3 (175B), Jurassic-1 (178B), and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B)," reaching 67.5% on MMLU (>7% over Gopher) (p. 1).
